title: XBOW Features in 2026: What the Autonomous Pentester Does and Where It Stops
summary: XBOW features checked against its own docs: how the agents work, what it tests, true-positive rates, reports, integrations and where it stops.
body_markdown:
XBOW (xbow.com) s an autonomous penetration testing platform for web applications and their APIs. Its AI agents map an app, attack it in parallel and report only findings a separate validator can reproduce, each with the working exploit. It retests fixes free and lets you generate auditor and engineering reports yourself, but it does not test cloud accounts, internal networks or Active Directory today. XBOW fits teams with many web apps to test all year; if you need one pentest across web, cloud and network assets with a report in 48 hours, CodeAnt AI is the closer match.


Last updated: November 13, 2026. Every XBOW fact below was checked on xbow.com, docs.xbow.com and XBOW's AWS Marketplace listing on that date.


> How we checked: we read XBOW's homepage, platform and pricing pages, its documentation (attack methods, authentication methods, asset types, reports, target protection, webhooks, data residency, organization admin), its AWS pages and its own blog posts on the HackerOne results and agent design. Where XBOW's marketing and its documentation say different things, we say so.


> **TL;DR:** XBOW’s strength is autonomous exploitation with proof. Thousands of short-lived attack agents map a target, chain vulnerabilities into working attacks, and a separate validation layer confirms exploitability before you see a finding, with zero false positives claimed in its published 1,060-attack study.


>


> The limits: it tests only web applications and their APIs, offers no SAST, SCA, secret scanning, or code review, never fixes code, runs SaaS-only, and gates SSO, API access, IDOR testing, and data residency behind the Enterprise tier. There is no free trial, and pricing went quote-only in mid-July 2026.


## What Is XBOW?


XBOW is an autonomous penetration testing platform that uses fleets of AI agents to find, chain, and exploit vulnerabilities in web applications, then delivers each validated finding with a proof-of-concept exploit. The company reached #1 on HackerOne’s US leaderboard above every human researcher and became the first autonomous system ranked on Microsoft’s MSRC leaderboard.


The platform sums up the workflow in two blunt sentences, “Point it at a URL. Get back working exploits.” Everything else in this breakdown is the machinery behind that promise.

## XBOW's Platform Page Describes Six Stages:


1.


Learn. You give XBOW context about the target: documentation, credentials, API specs, architecture notes or source code. It can start with none, but "the more context it has, the deeper it goes."


2.


Map. It builds a live map of the application's endpoints, parameters and login flows.


3.


Coordinate. A coordinator decides what to test, where and in what order, and directs what XBOW calls "thousands of agents."


4.


Attack. Agents work in parallel and chain weaknesses into working attacks.


5.


Prove. Independent validators confirm each exploit is reproducible before it becomes a finding.


6.


Verify. After you deploy a fix, XBOW retests it and confirms the issue is closed.


The agents are short-lived on purpose. In XBOW's July 2025 post on agent design, each "solver" gets one part of the attack surface and one bug class, runs for a fixed number of steps (80 in the experiments it describes), and is then replaced by a fresh solver that does not carry the old one's wrong assumptions. XBOW also routes tasks across models from different providers rather than relying on one.


Testing depth depends on what you hand over. XBOW says an assessment can run black box from a single URL or as full white box with source code, and that teams can add API specs, earlier pentest reports and priority endpoints, much as they would brief a human tester. Source code is used to guide attacks on the running application; XBOW does not list static code scanning, dependency scanning or secrets scanning among its products.


## What Does XBOW Need From Your Application?


XBOW's asset requirements are stricter than many buyers expect:


-


A complete environment, with no pending onboarding or setup steps.


-


More than one session per user at a time. Apps that cannot do this can run in Sequential mode, which takes longer.


-


Sessions that expire on inactivity rather than a short fixed timeout, so long tests can finish.


-


A login method XBOW supports and a modern Chrome-compatible front end.


-


Network access: XBOW's IP addresses must be allowed through, and assets behind a VPN cannot be tested.


Test apps, toy apps and environments seeded with test flags are listed as unsuitable. In practice this means a staging copy that looks like production, with two test accounts per role if you want XBOW to check whether one user can reach another user's data.


## How Accurate are XBOW's Findings?


XBOW separates finding a weakness from proving it. A finding reaches you only after a validator confirms the exploit can be reproduced, and findings in generally available classes are confirmed by a deterministic check. Each one comes with "the working exploit, the request, the response and the steps to reproduce it."


XBOW's documentation puts numbers on accuracy by release phase. Attack methods in general availability, which run in every comprehensive assessment, show over 90% true positive results in XBOW's internal testing. Public preview methods, which you switch on yourself, show over 70%. Private preview methods are available on request, and their findings are triaged by XBOW's internal security team before you see them. XBOW's homepage says findings "are reviewed before you see them," and its AWS page says every engagement includes a final review by a human security expert.


Two things follow for a buyer. First, ask which of your findings came from preview methods, because those carry a lower stated true positive rate. Second, do not rely on a single headline accuracy figure from any vendor: run the tool against an application your last pentest covered and compare what each one proved. XBOW suggests exactly that test on its own platform page.


## Is XBOW Just a Vulnerability Scanner?


No. A scanner pattern-matches versions and configurations and hands you possibilities, while XBOW exploits what it finds and hands you proof, drawing the line in its own words as “exploitation, not pattern-matching.”


The difference shows up in the deliverable. Every finding ships with a proof-of-concept exploit and a trace of the whole attack, request by request, where[DAST-style scanning](https://www.codeant.ai/blogs/ai-pentesting-vs-traditional-dast) leaves the validation burden on your team.


## What Attack Types Does XBOW Run?


The official docs list seven default attack types run in every comprehensive assessment: local file inclusion, remote code execution, cache poisoning, open redirect, server-side request forgery, cross-site scripting, and SQL injection. Layered on top are checks for public and private CVEs, SSL/TLS issues, default credentials, exposed tokens and config files, information disclosure, and other misconfigurations.


Findings are grouped by CWE as selected by NIST’s National Vulnerability Database, each carrying a maturity label of Validated, Informational, or Preview. Read the labels carefully, because missing-authorization findings (CWE-862) are a Validated class while several authentication weaknesses (CWE-287, CWE-306, CWE-863) are Informational-only.


Optional attack types sit at the Enterprise tier:[Insecure Direct Object References](https://www.codeant.ai/blogs/idor-vulnerabilities) in public preview, and application-specific custom canaries. Enterprise users can also narrow a run to a subset of attack types, while everyone else gets the full default set.


## How Does XBOW Handle Source Code and Testing Modes?


XBOW tests in[blackbox, whitebox, or greybox](https://www.codeant.ai/blogs/black-box-vs-white-box-vs-gray-box-penetration-testing) modes, and in the whitebox and greybox cases you can upload source code as additional context for evaluating findings and selecting payloads. Reports then include the relevant code context.


Read that carefully, because it is the most misunderstood XBOW capability. Source code is an input that sharpens runtime attacks, never an asset that gets scanned, so there is no static analysis pass, no repository connection, and no code-level findings.


The distinction between that and[SAST](https://www.codeant.ai/blogs/what-is-sast) decides which half of the problem you have covered.


## What Does XBOW's HackerOne Ranking Mean?


In June 2025 XBOW reached the top of HackerOne's US leaderboard, the first autonomous system to do so. XBOW's own write-up gives the detail behind it: nearly 1,060 vulnerability reports submitted, of which 130 were resolved, 303 triaged, 208 marked duplicate, 209 informative and 36 not applicable, with the rest new or awaiting review. XBOW's security team reviewed reports before submission, as HackerOne's policy on automated tools requires. Its homepage now claims the #1 spot with "1,500+ reproducible exploits on production targets" and first place on Microsoft's MSRC leaderboard with three critical CVEs.


What that tells you: XBOW's agents find real, reportable bugs on public programs at scale, and the duplicate and informative counts show the same noise human bug hunters see. What it does not tell you is how XBOW will do on your application, behind your login, against your business logic. Treat the leaderboard as evidence the engine works, then judge it on a test of your own app.


## Is XBOW safe to run against production?


XBOW is built to test production and staging, with several layers of control:


-


Scope configuration and protected URLs decide what XBOW may touch.


-


A command checker blocks destructive actions, and every action is logged.


-


Target protection sets how much risk XBOW may accept. Standard, the default, avoids actions that could disrupt the asset or lock the accounts it uses. Permissive allows wider actions to prove impact, such as running operating system commands through a SQL injection or changing settings after a remote code execution. At both levels XBOW never deletes or updates database records, never sends data outside your boundary, never runs denial-of-service-style actions and never moves from a finding into other services. Target protection is in public preview.


-


You can set rate limits and testing windows, tag XBOW's traffic with custom headers, and pause at any time.


XBOW recommends a staged start: unauthenticated external testing first, then targeted and authenticated runs. If your application moves money or triggers workflows from ordinary POST requests, test a staging copy first whatever the vendor's safeguards.


## What reports does XBOW produce, and do they cover compliance?


XBOW's platform page says it supports "40+ frameworks" and names SOC 2, ISO 27001, ISO 42001, PCI DSS, NIS 2, HIPAA and GDPR. Its report documentation describes three formats, all generated by you from the same dated snapshot of findings:


-


Letter of attestation: what was assessed, when and how, with finding counts by severity, status and OWASP weakness category, and no exploitable detail. Written for auditors and customers.


-


Executive summary: adds the critical and high findings with CVSS scores and status, for internal leadership.


-


Full penetration testing report: every finding with reproduction steps, for security and engineering teams.


Since October 30, 2026, XBOW also creates a report automatically after each successful comprehensive assessment or retest, covering that assessment alone. Reports leave out findings still awaiting XBOW staff triage and findings you mark as intended behavior.


The gap to check: the report documentation names the OWASP category as its only framework reference, while the marketing names seven frameworks. Before you buy for an audit, send a sample attestation letter to your auditor and ask whether it meets their evidence request. The OWASP Top 10 itself is an awareness document, not a compliance standard, so the mapping your auditor needs may go further.


## Can XBOW send findings and events to other systems?


Yes, through four routes, all configured by an organization Administrator:


-


The XBOW API, to register assets, start assessments and pull findings. The reference is titled "XBOW API Reference (Preview)" and is versioned, with 2026-11-01 the latest.


-


Webhooks for asset.changed (credentials or testing windows change), assessment.changed (status changes, useful for completed or failed alerts) and finding.changed (for example open to fixed). XBOW sends two test pings on setup, one signed with its real key and one with an invalid key, so you can check your signature validation.


-


Jira, to create work items from findings with optional write-back of workflow state (public preview).


-


Microsoft Sentinel and Security Copilot, to send findings to a Log Analytics workspace and run assessments from Security Copilot (public preview).


XBOW's platform page also mentions sending findings to GitHub issues and coding agents.


## What do customers say about XBOW?


Independent reviews are thin. As of November 13, 2026, XBOW has no reviews on G2. The customer evidence available is what XBOW publishes: testimonials on its homepage, a Fortune 50 customer that assessed 180 applications in a month with 1,216 validated findings, and a claim of "200+ top security teams" as users. Those are vendor-selected, so treat them as a reason to shortlist, not as proof.


If customer feedback matters to your decision, ask XBOW for two references in your industry who have used it for more than one assessment cycle, and ask them about false positives on logged-in testing, how quickly support answered, and whether their auditor accepted the attestation letter.


## Where Does XBOW Stop?


-


**Web apps and APIs only.** Cloud accounts, Kubernetes, internal networks and Active Directory are outside its scope today, so an audit that covers them needs a second test.


-


**Login limits.** SMS codes, Google login, CAPTCHA and self-registration flows are not supported, and XBOW usually needs to log in before it can test.


-


**Demanding targets.** Apps need concurrent sessions or a slower Sequential mode, activity-based session expiry and reachable, allowlisted network access.


-


**Several features are still preview.** The API, the Jira and Microsoft integrations, SSO, user provisioning, target protection and data residency all carry a preview label in the docs.


-


**One target class.** Official docs scope testing to web applications and their APIs, with other target types on the roadmap, which leaves mobile apps, networks, cloud configuration, and infrastructure to other tools, mapped in our[alternatives roundup](https://www.codeant.ai/blogs/xbow-alternatives) .


-


**The code-security half is absent.** No SAST, no[software composition analysis](https://www.codeant.ai/blogs/what-is-software-composition-analysis-sca) , no secret scanning, no IaC checks, no code review, and no repo connection. XBOW proves your deployed app is exploitable and has no opinion on the pull request that made it so.


-


**Report mapping is thin in the docs.** Check the attestation letter with your auditor before relying on it for SOC 2, PCI DSS or HIPAA evidence.


-


**No public price.** XBOW quotes usage-based pricing; the AWS Marketplace listing shows a $50,000 12-month credit package with non-refundable fees, and a free trial on terms XBOW sets. See our XBOW pricing breakdown for the detail.


-


**Your engineers still fix.** XBOW gives a fix suggestion with each finding and retests your fix; it does not change your code.


-


**The gates are steep.** SSO, API access, IDOR coverage, attack-type selection, and data residency all require Enterprise, and since mid-July 2026 there is no published price, no trial, and no self-serve path, covered in full in our[XBOW pricing breakdown](https://www.codeant.ai/blogs/xbow-pricing) .

## What Should You Ask Before Buying an Autonomous Pentest?


These questions come up on our own sales calls, paraphrased. They apply to any autonomous pentest, XBOW included.


-


"What is your false positive rate?" Buyers who have used AI code bots that are right most of the time but not always want a number. Ask for it per finding class and per release phase, not one headline figure, and ask how many of your findings came from preview methods.


-


"Does autonomous mean nobody checks logged-in roles?" Many serious bugs sit after login: one tenant reading another tenant's data, a low-privilege user reaching admin actions. Ask which login methods the tool supports, whether it tests with two accounts per role, and who reviews those findings.


-


"Who do we talk to when something breaks?" Enterprise teams often do not want to log in to another dashboard every day. They want someone to alert them, explain a finding and help through remediation. Ask what support looks like during and after the test, not only in the sales cycle.


-


"Will it find assets we did not list?" A domain-based test finds what is reachable from that domain. Internal IP ranges that are not linked to it will not appear unless you put them in scope, so list them explicitly.


## Where This Leaves You


XBOW’s feature set is a focused, publicly validated attack engine: a five-stage autonomous loop, real exploit chains, deterministic validation, and compliance-mapped reports, aimed exclusively at web applications and their APIs. The caveats are the missing code layer, the preview-stage integrations, the Enterprise gating, and a buying process that now starts with a form instead of a price.


Pick by the gap you are covering.


If it is the deployed web app, XBOW belongs on your shortlist, with costs examined in the[pricing breakdown](https://www.codeant.ai/blogs/xbow-pricing) and rivals in the[alternatives guide](https://www.codeant.ai/blogs/xbow-alternatives) . If the gap runs from the code outward, CodeAnt AI covers both halves and starts proving exploits on a URL[for free today](https://www.codeant.ai/pentesting) .
